kernelIdea: ℤ is closed under addition, additive inverses, and multiplication, and satisfies the distributive law — this makes it a ring. It is not closed under multiplicative inverses: only 1 and −1 have integer reciprocals.

kernels.l1: Adding whole piles keeps them whole. Sharing them out does not.
kernels.l2: Adding and multiplying whole numbers always gives you back a whole number. Dividing can throw you out of the whole numbers altogether.
kernels.l3: The integers are closed under adding, taking the opposite, and multiplying — those operations never take you outside. Dividing does, so the integers are missing something.
kernels.l4: ℤ is closed under addition, additive inverses, and multiplication, and satisfies the distributive law. It is not closed under multiplicative inverses: only 1 and −1 have integer reciprocals.
kernels.l5: Closure under +, −, and × plus distributivity makes ℤ a ring; failure of multiplicative inverses is what stops it being a field.
kernels.l6: ℤ is a commutative ring with identity; the same axioms govern polynomials and square matrices, which is why the word ring earns its keep.
kernels.l7: ℤ is closed under addition, negation, and multiplication and satisfies the distributive law, making it a commutative ring with identity; only ±1 are units, so ℤ is not a field.
kernels.l8: ℤ is an integral domain whose units are ±1; the ring axioms are exactly the properties used in every integer proof, and abstraction of them is the starting point of algebra.
